name: Pedro Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you tell me is confidential and won't be linked to your name. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at the Campus Health Centre at the university, so most of my patients are eighteen to twenty-five, plus the staff. Mornings are walk-ins: chest infections, contraception, anxiety before exams, sprained ankles from five-a-side. I use an AI note-taker in every appointment and a triage tool that sorts the online requests before we open. I'm quick, but I'm sloppy sometimes, and Dr Kowalczyk, my supervisor, catches things I miss more often than I'd like.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you enjoy, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I enjoy the pace and the variety, and I like tinkering with how the clinic runs. I built a little set of AI prompts that turns my notes into patient leaflets in plain language, and three other doctors now use it. What wears me out is exam season, when half the campus has panic attacks and we have two counsellors. At home it's me and my partner Hana, who tests software for a games company, and we're both a bit obsessed with our savings spreadsheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fair enough, the hype was bigger than the product. I'd still say the tools we've got are worth having, because the note-taker gives me back about an hour a day. Online I'd probably post something dry about all the startups that just lost their funding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's fine, slightly boring. My job's secure, the university isn't going anywhere, and I've got good savings in index funds. Hana's job is probably safer in this world too, which is nice, because testing software is exactly the kind of work the hype was aimed at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep doing what I'm doing and keep using the tools I already use. I'd keep putting a third of my pay into index funds every month, same as now. And I'd keep tinkering with the leaflet prompts, because even a plateau has room for small wins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. A little disappointed. Mostly I'd shrug and get on with it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the note-taker gives you an hour a day. Where does that hour go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Partly to patients, partly to going home on time. During exam season I spend it on the students with panic attacks, because fifteen minutes isn't enough for someone shaking. An hour a day back from typing is an hour I can spend on a frightened nineteen-year-old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything in this picture that would still bother you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The counselling waits, which are a people problem, not a tech problem. And prices: if nothing changes, our flat deposit keeps running away from us, because prices near the university keep climbing. That's the boring worry in the boring world.

say: The hype was **bigger than the product**, and that's fair enough.
The **note-taker** is still worth having, because it gives me back an hour a day.
think: My **job and savings** are secure at a university that isn't going anywhere.
Hana's **testing job** is probably safer in this world too.
do: Keep using the **note-taker** and triage tool as I do now.
Keep putting a **third of my pay** into index funds each month.
Keep improving my **leaflet prompts** for plain-language patient advice.
feel: **Calm** and a little disappointed, ready to shrug and carry on.
S0.quote: An hour a day back from typing is an hour I can spend on a frightened nineteen-year-old.
fieldNote: He is already a **daily AI user** who builds small tools for colleagues.
His remaining worries are **counselling waits** and rising prices near campus.
He thinks about his household as a **savings spreadsheet**, shared with his partner.

steps.text: Keep using the AI note-taker and triage tool at the campus clinic
Put a third of his pay into index funds each month
Refine his AI prompts that turn notes into patient leaflets

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for patients if we do it properly, and I'd say it at work, loudly. I'd offer to help the Campus Health Centre set up the tools for everyone, not just me. Online I'd probably share a post about the leaflet prompts and how much time they save.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, it's good for me. I'm already the doctor who uses this stuff, so I'd become more useful, not less. The worry is Hana: her games company has already cut two testers this year and replaced them with an AI that plays the game a thousand times overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer to lead the AI rollout at the centre in the first six months: triage, letters, booking, the lot. I'd say yes to a small health-tech startup that's been asking me to advise them one evening a month, which would bring in a bit extra. And I'd move some savings into a broad fund that includes the AI companies, because if this is happening, I'd rather own a slice of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly excited. A bit uneasy about Hana. I'd feel like the tide was finally coming in my direction.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Hana the night she heard about more cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell her we're fine on my pay for a long while, and that she should start learning to build the testing AI rather than compete with it. She'd roll her eyes, because I say that about everything. But I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd own a slice of it. Isn't that a strange thing for a doctor to say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I'd rather be honest about it. If the AI companies are going to earn from replacing work, including my partner's, I'd rather some of that money came back to our household. Better that than none of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is too fast for the health system and it needs rules immediately: who's responsible when the AI is wrong, and what happens to the staff. I'd be practical about it at work, not dramatic. Online I'd say we should plan for it, not pretend it isn't coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think doctors who can work with the AI survive, and I'm one of them. By 2028 most of the diagnosis and the paperwork is the AI's, and I'd be supervising it and doing the examinations until robots arrive around 2031. Hana's job, though, is almost certainly gone, and our household drops to one income just as we wanted to buy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go part-time at the centre and take a paid role as clinical safety lead at the health-tech startup, checking their AI before it reaches patients. I'd keep the flat plan on hold and build a year and a half of costs in cash. And I'd help Hana pay for a course in something hands-on or in building the AI tools, whichever she picks.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, more than I'd show. I'm fine, but we're not fine as two people until Hana lands somewhere. I'd still feel I had a plan, which helps.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you're fine, but you're also building a cash cushion. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Both. I'm fine as a doctor, but a household that loses half its income in two years isn't fine. The cash is for us, not for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I've got until about 2031 where the hands-on part of medicine, examinations, stitches, a hand on a shoulder, is still mine. The AI would beat me at diagnosis by 2028, but a robot won't put a hand on a student's shoulder until 2031. I'd use those three years to make myself the one who runs the AI, not the one it replaces.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a decent runway and every practice should use it: train staff, write the rules, and decide now what doctors are for. I'd keep saying it in meetings and online, in a calm, numbers-first way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, five years is almost ideal. I'd finish training by 2029 and have two years as a qualified doctor plus two years advising a startup. Hana has time to switch into something safer, and the hands-on part of my work lasts until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd add sports and exercise medicine to my training, because the campus has a huge sports programme and it's very hands-on: joints, muscles, injections. I'd keep moving savings into a mix of index funds and property, so we're not relying only on wages by 2031. And I'd keep building my own AI tools at the clinic, so by 2031 I know the systems inside out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy but mostly positive. It feels like a hill I can climb. I'd sleep fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why property, in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because when wages get shaky, owning something real helps. A small flat near the university always rents to students, and boring is what you want when everything else is moving.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a first-year medical student at the university, in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell a first-year medical student to learn the hands-on stuff properly and to use the AI every single day. The doctors who do both will be fine in 2031, and the ones who do neither will struggle. I'd say it to them in the clinic, between the ankle sprains.

We must decide now **what doctors are for** when AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty, and people who panic now are wasting energy. I'd say plan steadily: skills, savings, rules. That's what I'd tell anyone at the clinic who asked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me, it's mostly good. I'd be thirty-seven in 2036, a well-established doctor with savings, maybe a rental flat, and years of experience running AI in a clinic. Hana would have ten years to move into something that suits her, and honestly she might end up building the AI tools herself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on with training and the clinic, no drama. I'd keep investing every month and keep the startup advising going as a side income. In about five years I'd sit down with Hana and redo the whole plan, because the picture will be clearer by 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Interested, even. Ten years is enough to be on the right side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anyone you'd worry about at the Campus Health Centre in this version?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The admin team and the older nurses who hate screens. There are four of them, and they'd have ten years, which is plenty if someone helps them. I'd offer to run sessions, because I'm the one who likes this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the right side of it. Is there a wrong side?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes. People who don't own anything and whose work is all thinking are on the wrong side of AI, even with ten years. Ten years helps them, but only if they start early. I'd rather say that honestly than pretend everyone comes out fine.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because of Hana more than me. Two years isn't long enough for her to switch careers, and we'd be on one income just as we wanted to buy. What would help is proper retraining support for people in thinking jobs like hers, paid while they learn, not after they've lost everything.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe whether people like me are part of the problem. I'm helping roll this stuff out and investing in it. I think a doctor who rolls out the AI should also help the people it pushes out, or he's just cashing in.

headlineQuote: A doctor who rolls out the AI should also help the people it pushes out, or he's just cashing in.
portrait: Pedro is a **27-year-old junior doctor** at a university's Campus Health Centre, seeing mostly students.
He uses **AI tools daily**, builds his own prompts and would lead his clinic's rollout.
He lives with Hana, a **software tester**, and invests a third of his pay.
His mood stays **calm or uneasy** for himself but turns anxious when Hana's job is at risk.
He's **pragmatic** about money, would advise a health-tech startup and admits he might be cashing in.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his partner couldn't switch careers in time and they'd drop to one income.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid retraining** for people in thinking jobs, while they learn rather than after losing everything.
